column1: What single physical fact determines whether a gain change is heard as a click/distortion versus a smooth volume move?
column2: Gain changes under ~1 ms are heard as clicks/distortion (inject audible high-frequency energy); gain changes spread over 50–200 ms are heard as a smooth, musical volume pull.

column1: What is the formula for gain reduction in dB given a signal's level above threshold and the ratio?
column2: Gain reduction (dB) = (dB above threshold) × (1 − 1/ratio). Example: 12 dB over threshold at 4:1 = 12 × 0.75 = 9 dB reduction.

column1: What ratio range technically turns a compressor into a limiter?
column2: Ratio ≥ 10:1 (often described as starting around 10:1, fully limiting above ~20:1), typically paired with fast/lookahead attack, so output essentially stops rising no matter how hard the input is driven.

column1: In a compressor's signal flow, why are the detector (sidechain) circuit and the main audio path kept separate?
column2: The sidechain analyzes the signal to decide how much gain reduction to apply, while the main path is where that reduction is actually multiplied onto the audio. This separation is what enables sidechain filtering, external sidechain inputs, and de-essing — the detector can listen to something different from what gets gain-reduced.

column1: Why does a compressor use an envelope follower instead of reacting to the instantaneous waveform?
column2: Raw audio crosses zero and swings wildly thousands of times per second; reacting to every zero-crossing would make the gain stage buzz and distort. The envelope follower smooths the signal over a few milliseconds into something resembling perceived loudness, which is what threshold/ratio actually act on.

column1: What is the difference between hard knee and soft knee compression?
column2: Hard knee: the full ratio engages instantly at threshold — surgical, obvious onset. Soft knee: ratio ramps up gradually over a few dB around threshold, hiding the onset of gain reduction — the default choice for vocals and mix-bus compression.

column1: Why must you A/B compressed vs. dry signal at matched loudness rather than matched fader position?
column2: Because louder audio is perceptually judged as 'better' even when only loudness (not quality) differs — matching loudness via makeup gain is required to judge tone/compression effect fairly.

column1: How do an expander and a gate relate to each other mechanically?
column2: They run the same engine: both reduce gain below a threshold. An expander uses a gentle ratio (e.g., 1.5:1) for subtle level reduction; a gate is expansion pushed to an extreme ratio (10:1, 20:1, or ∞:1) so it behaves almost like an on/off switch.

column1: What does the Hold parameter do on a gate, and why is it needed?
column2: Hold sets the minimum time the gate stays open once triggered, before release begins. It prevents chatter (rapid re-triggering) on sources with a slow natural decay, such as toms or cymbals.

column1: Why does noise become audible only in the gaps between notes, not while the wanted signal plays?
column2: Simultaneous masking: the noise floor (hiss, hum, bleed) is inaudible while the loud wanted signal is present, but becomes obvious once the wanted signal stops — expansion/gating prevent you from ever hearing the noise alone.

column1: On 1176-style compressors (e.g., CLA-76, UAD 1176), how is the Attack knob numbered, and what control replaces Threshold?
column2: Attack runs ~20–800 microseconds, with 7 being the FASTEST setting and 1 the SLOWEST (reversed from intuition). There is no threshold knob; instead, the Input knob sets how hard the detector is driven, and Ratio is a button set (4, 8, 12, 20, All).

column1: Why does tempo-syncing a compressor's release time (e.g., to an 1/8 note) reduce the perceived problem of pumping?
column2: Fast release settings cause gain to pump audibly in time with the music; syncing release to the song's BPM makes that rhythmic breathing feel intentional and musical rather than like a broken artifact.
